warmup.q: A Java service needs handlers for PaymentCaptured. The Kotlin bus offers fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>) and inline fun <reified E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(handler: Handler<E>). What can the Java team write?
options: Nothing: Java can't call either function
warmup.why: A Class is not a KClass, so the first call doesn't match. The reified function is compiled as a synthetic method, and javac ignores synthetic methods, so the second finds nothing. The KClass version is callable once Java converts the class by hand, which works and reads badly. This lesson adds a Class<E> overload so Java can write the first line.

sections.h: A subscription DSL: one block, one handle
sections.html:
Wiring a service by hand looks like this: five subscribe calls, five handles to keep, and a config lookup between the third and the fourth. If that lookup throws, three handlers are live, nobody holds their handles, and the service starts half wired. The fix is the DSL shape from Type-safe DSLs with lambdas with receivers: a builder that collects what the block declares, and an entry function that commits it all at once.

Java
// Java, through the Consumer entry point
Subscription handle = Events.subscriptions(bus, timings, b -> {
    b.on(PaymentEvent.class, e -> audit.record(e));
    b.on(PaymentCaptured.class, Handlers.timed(c -> ledger.credit(c), "ledger", timings));
    b.on(PaymentRefunded.class, Handlers.timed(r -> ledger.debit(r), "ledger", timings));
});
Kotlin
val handle = bus.subscriptions(timings) {
    on<PaymentEvent> { audit.record(it) }
    timed("ledger") {
        on<PaymentCaptured> { ledger.credit(it) }
        on<PaymentRefunded> { ledger.debit(it) }
    }
}

Each piece is a decision. on only adds a Pending(type, handler) to a list; commit subscribes them after the block has returned. So a block that throws subscribes nothing, and the caller gets back one Subscription that closes everything, in reverse order. Pending<E> keeps a type and its handler together, so the builder can hold a List<Pending<*>> and still subscribe each entry without a cast, using the star projection from Star projection: when you don't know the type.

on<PaymentCaptured> { ... } is inline with a reified E, so it can pass E::class on, as in Type erasure and reified type parameters. Its body is on(E::class, Handler { handler(it) }), and the compiler stops you there: cannot inline 'handler: (E) -> Unit' here: it might contain non-local returns. Add 'crossinline' modifier. The lambda is called from inside another object, the Handler, which runs later, when no enclosing function is left to return from. Inline functions: noinline, crossinline and non-local returns gave the choice: noinline would also compile but keeps a lambda object inside the Handler; crossinline pastes the body into the generated Handler class.

One mistake the DSL can't prevent at compile time: calling on from inside a handler. The handler lambda has no receiver, so the builder is still in scope, and the call compiles. At run time it would register into a builder that has already committed, and the subscription would silently never exist. A check(!committed) in on turns that into an IllegalStateException at the first event, which the bus's isolation reports.

Before you run the demo, predict the handler count it prints after the block that fails.

code.title: DslDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.events.l03.demo.dsl import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList import java.util.function.Consumer import kotlin.reflect.KClass import kotlin.reflect.cast // A compact copy of the library: plain ids and cents, a flat-list bus, timing, and the DSL. sealed interface PaymentEvent { val paymentId: String } data class PaymentAuthorized(override val paymentId: String, val cents: Long) : PaymentEvent data class PaymentCaptured(override val paymentId: String, val cents: Long) : PaymentEvent data class PaymentRefunded(override val paymentId: String, val cents: Long) : PaymentEvent fun interface Handler<in E : PaymentEvent> { fun handle(event: E) } fun interface Subscription : AutoCloseable { override fun close() } class Bus { private val handlers = CopyOnWriteArrayList<Pair<KClass<*>, Handler<PaymentEvent>>>() fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { val entry = type to Handler<PaymentEvent> { handler.handle(type.cast(it)) } handlers += entry return Subscription { handlers -= entry } } fun publish(event: PaymentEvent) = handlers.filter { it.first.isInstance(event) }.forEach { it.second.handle(event) } fun handlerCount() = handlers.size } class Timings { var clock = 0L // virtual time: each read moves it 2 ms val calls = mutableMapOf<String, Int>() val millis = mutableMapOf<String, Long>() fun tick(): Long { clock += 2_000_000; return clock } } fun <E : PaymentEvent> Handler<E>.timed(name: String, t: Timings): Handler<E> = Handler { e -> val start = t.tick() try { handle(e) } finally { t.calls.merge(name, 1) { a, b -> a + b } t.millis.merge(name, (t.tick() - start) / 1_000_000) { a, b -> a + b } } } @DslMarker @Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS) annotation class EventsDsl @EventsDsl class SubscriptionsBuilder(private val bus: Bus, private val timings: Timings) { private val pending = mutableListOf<() -> Subscription>() fun <E : PaymentEvent> on(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>) { pending += { bus.subscribe(type, handler) } } fun <E : PaymentEvent> on(type: Class<E>, handler: Handler<E>) = on(type.kotlin, handler) inline fun <reified E : PaymentEvent> on(crossinline handler: (E) -> Unit) = on(E::class, Handler { handler(it) }) fun timed(name: String, block: TimedGroup.() -> Unit) = TimedGroup(name, timings, this).block() fun commit(): Subscription { val handles = pending.map { it() } // subscribe only after the block has finished return Subscription { handles.asReversed().forEach(Subscription::close) } } } @EventsDsl class TimedGroup(private val name: String, private val timings: Timings, private val parent: SubscriptionsBuilder) { fun <E : PaymentEvent> on(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>) = parent.on(type, handler.timed(name, timings)) fun <E : PaymentEvent> on(type: Class<E>, handler: Handler<E>) = on(type.kotlin, handler) inline fun <reified E : PaymentEvent> on(crossinline handler: (E) -> Unit) = on(E::class, Handler { handler(it) }) } /** The Kotlin entry point. */ fun Bus.subscriptions(timings: Timings, block: SubscriptionsBuilder.() -> Unit): Subscription = SubscriptionsBuilder(this, timings).apply(block).commit() /** The Java entry point: a Consumer, so Java lambdas need no return Unit.INSTANCE. */ object JavaDsl { @JvmStatic fun subscriptions(bus: Bus, timings: Timings, block: Consumer<SubscriptionsBuilder>): Subscription = bus.subscriptions(timings) { block.accept(this) } } fun main() { val bus = Bus() val timings = Timings() val handle = bus.subscriptions(timings) { on<PaymentEvent> { println("audit ${it.paymentId} ${it::class.simpleName}") } timed("ledger") { on<PaymentCaptured> { println("ledger +${it.cents}") } on<PaymentRefunded> { println("ledger -${it.cents}") } } } bus.publish(PaymentCaptured("pay_7781", 1_999)) bus.publish(PaymentRefunded("pay_7781", 500)) bus.publish(PaymentAuthorized("pay_7782", 250)) println("ledger: ${timings.calls["ledger"]} calls, ${timings.millis["ledger"]} ms; handlers: ${bus.handlerCount()}") handle.close() println("after close: ${bus.handlerCount()} handlers") try { bus.subscriptions(timings) { on<PaymentCaptured> { println("never subscribed") } error("missing configuration: ledger account") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("block failed (${e.message}); handlers: ${bus.handlerCount()}") } }

alt.title: DslDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.events.l03.demo.dsl; import kotlin.Unit; /** The same wiring as DslDemo.kt, written in Java against the Kotlin DSL in that file. */ public class DslDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Bus bus = new Bus(); Timings timings = new Timings(); Subscription handle = JavaDsl.subscriptions(bus, timings, b -> { // a Consumer: void lambda b.on(PaymentEvent.class, e -> System.out.println("audit " + e.getPaymentId() + " " + e.getClass().getSimpleName())); b.timed("ledger", g -> { // a Function1: the price of a g.on(PaymentCaptured.class, c -> System.out.println("ledger +" + c.getCents())); // receiver lambda g.on(PaymentRefunded.class, r -> System.out.println("ledger -" + r.getCents())); return Unit.INSTANCE; }); }); bus.publish(new PaymentCaptured("pay_7781", 1_999)); bus.publish(new PaymentRefunded("pay_7781", 500)); bus.publish(new PaymentAuthorized("pay_7782", 250)); System.out.println("ledger: " + timings.getCalls().get("ledger") + " calls, " + timings.getMillis().get("ledger") + " ms; handlers: " + bus.handlerCount()); handle.close(); // close() throws nothing System.out.println("after close: " + bus.handlerCount() + " handlers"); try { JavaDsl.subscriptions(bus, timings, b -> { b.on(PaymentCaptured.class, c -> System.out.println("never subscribed")); throw new IllegalStateException("missing configuration: ledger account"); }); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("block failed (" + e.getMessage() + "); handlers: " + bus.handlerCount()); } } }

try.expect: ledger: 2 calls, 4 ms; handlers: 3, then after close: 0 handlers and block failed (missing configuration: ledger account); handlers: 0. With your eager on, the handle has nothing to close, so you get after close: 3 handlers, and the failed block leaves one more behind: handlers: 4. In the Java twin, Unit.INSTANCE appears only inside b.timed(...), which takes a Kotlin receiver lambda; the Consumer entry point needs none.

sections.h: @DslMarker keeps a nested block from reaching out
sections.html:
Inside timed("ledger") { ... } two builders are in scope: the TimedGroup (nearest) and the SubscriptionsBuilder around it. Kotlin resolves a call against both, nearest first. TimedGroup has no timed, so this compiles:

Java
// Java has no implicit receivers: the same mistake must name the outer builder, b
b.timed("ledger", g -> {
    g.on(PaymentCaptured.class, c -> ledger.credit(c));
    b.timed("refunds", r -> { r.on(PaymentRefunded.class, e -> ledger.debit(e)); return Unit.INSTANCE; });
    return Unit.INSTANCE;
});
Kotlin
timed("ledger") {
    on<PaymentCaptured> { ledger.credit(it) }
    timed("refunds") { on<PaymentRefunded> { ledger.debit(it) } }   // reaches the OUTER builder
}

You meant "refunds, inside the ledger group". What you get is a sibling group: refunds are timed under refunds only, and the ledger dashboard silently misses them. The demo prints {ledger=1, refunds=1} where you expected the ledger to count two.

Mark both builder classes with an annotation that is itself annotated @DslMarker, and the nested call stops compiling: 'fun timed(name: String, block: TimedGroup.() -> Unit): Unit' cannot be called in this context with an implicit receiver. Use an explicit receiver if necessary. If you really want a sibling, say so with a label, this@subscriptions.timed("refunds") { ... }, which nobody types by accident. The rules are the ones from that DSL lesson: the marker counts on classes (or a common superclass), and has no effect on functions.

Java never had this problem. Every Java lambda names its parameter, so reaching the outer builder takes b.timed, and a reviewer sees it. Java pays elsewhere: timed takes a TimedGroup.() -> Unit, which Java sees as Function1<TimedGroup, Unit>, so each block ends with return Unit.INSTANCE. That cost is why the Java entry point, Events.subscriptions, takes a java.util.function.Consumer, and why the lab's Java code times handlers with Handlers.timed(...) instead of a group.

In the demo, uncomment the nested timed, run, then delete @DslMarker and predict the printed map.

sections.h: What Java sees, and the surface that fixes it
sections.html:
Here is what javac sees when Java code meets the API as Kotlin developers usually write it. Every error below is from the demo:

Kotlin as written What Java gets The fix
inline fun <reified E> subscribe(h) invisible: no suitable method found for subscribe((e)->{ }) a Class<E> overload
fun <E> subscribe(type: KClass<E>, h) callable via JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(X.class) the same overload
constructor with defaults new PlainBus() and the full one only: no suitable constructor found for PlainBus(String) @JvmOverloads
object member Registry.INSTANCE.publish(...) @JvmStatic
companion val SYSTEM Ticker.Companion.getSYSTEM() @JvmField
top-level functions in Timing.kt TimingKt.timed(...) @file:JvmName("Handlers")
data class with value-class properties PaymentCaptured(String,long) has private access, getters like getAmount-M68TK6M() a facade

The facade is the decision that matters, because it touches validation. Value classes and what they compile to showed that @JvmName on a function that takes a value class lets Java pass a raw long straight past init. The facade does the opposite: it takes plain values and builds the value classes, so every init block runs.

Java
PaymentCaptured c = Events.captured("pay_7781", 1_999);   // validates: "7781" throws
long cents = Events.amountMinor(c);
bus.subscribe(PaymentCaptured.class, e -> ledger.credit(Events.paymentId(e), Events.amountMinor(e)));
Kotlin
object Events {
    @JvmStatic
    fun captured(paymentId: String, amountMinor: Long): PaymentCaptured =
        PaymentCaptured(PaymentId(paymentId), Money(amountMinor))       // init blocks run

    @JvmStatic
    fun amountMinor(event: MoneyMovement): Long = event.amount.minor
}

@JvmExposeBoxed (Experimental in Kotlin 2.4, opt-in) would give Java new PaymentCaptured(new PaymentId(...), new Money(...)) and a boxed getAmount(). In a quick test with its module-wide flag, the getter on the PaymentEvent interface itself stayed mangled, so Java code that only knows PaymentEvent would still need Events.paymentId(e). Keep the facade until that changes.

Some of the Java surface came for free from earlier decisions. Lesson 2's Handler<in E> shows up as Handler<? super E>, so a Java Handler<PaymentEvent> fits any subscription. kotlinc writes PermittedSubclasses for the sealed model, so a Java switch over a PaymentEvent with one case per leaf compiles with no default. Subscription.close() declares no checked exception, so try-with-resources needs no catch. And because handlers and middleware are fun interfaces with void and int methods, Java lambdas never return Unit.INSTANCE.

Uncomment the four lines at the end of JavaViewDemo.java one at a time and predict javac's complaint before each run.

sections.h: Design review: defend it, or undo it
sections.html:
A design review is where you find out which decisions you can defend. Here are the questions a sceptical reviewer asks about this library, with the answer I'd give. Disagree where your service differs.

"Why value classes, if Java needs a facade?" Keep them. In the Kotlin model a swapped id and amount don't compile, and an invalid id can't exist. The facade costs one file. If most callers were Java, I'd undo it and use plain records with compact constructors.

"Money has no currency." Undo it before a second currency arrives. Money(minor, currency) becomes a data class, one object per amount, and the edge gets a currency field to parse. The one-field rule of value classes made the first version cheap; it doesn't make it right forever.

"Supertype dispatch will surprise people." Keep it, and document it. The sealed hierarchy makes the set of keys small, fixed and testable, and the order is a tested promise. The surprise to warn about: a PaymentEvent handler also receives every event type added next year.

"in, adapters, casts: isn't that over-engineered?" Keep in: it is what lets one audit handler serve every subscription, from Kotlin and from Java. The single cast is checked by type.cast and guaranteed by the keys.

"Delivery is synchronous and in memory." Keep it for decoupling modules inside one service. Undo it for anything that must survive a crash or reach another service: that goes to an outbox table and Kafka. Guava's own EventBus Javadoc now says "We recommend against using EventBus", and lists no backpressure, little control of threading and no exception propagation among the reasons. This bus fixes the last one with an ErrorHandler, and not the first two.

"DropDuplicates remembers every event forever." Undo it as written. Bound it to a window of recent events, or move idempotency into the handler's own store with a unique key, which also survives restarts.

"The DSL commits after the block. What if commit fails halfway?" Today subscribe can't fail. If it ever can, commit must close what it already opened before rethrowing.

Notice the pattern in the answers. A choice is safe when an earlier lesson's mechanism forces it (in for a consumer, no else on a sealed when). It is a judgment call when it trades cost for safety (value classes, the facade, a currency-less Money). Those are the ones to write down, with the condition that would make you undo them.

try.title: Write your own review notes
steps: Without looking back, list five design choices in the library you built across the three labs.
For each, write one line: keep or undo, the earlier lesson whose mechanism decides it, and the condition that would change your answer.
Pick the choice you're least sure about and write the test that would tell you you were wrong.
try.expect: A strong list mixes forced choices (no else on the sealed when, Handler<in E>, a Class<E> overload because Java can't call reified functions) with judgment calls (value classes plus a facade, euro-only Money, synchronous delivery, unbounded dedupe). The forced ones cite a mechanism; the judgment calls cite a condition, such as "undo when a second currency arrives" or "undo when a handler needs to survive a restart".

refs.title: Guava EventBus Javadoc: why Guava recommends against it

analogy: Think of a bank branch with one vault and two counters. At the first counter, regulars speak the house shorthand and the teller fills in the forms for them: that's the Kotlin DSL. At the second, visitors fill in the standard printed forms themselves: that's the Java door, with its overloads and its facade. Both counters feed the same vault, under the same rules. The analogy breaks where a teller might bend a rule for a visitor who doesn't understand the form. The facade never may: Events.captured builds the same value classes and runs the same checks as the Kotlin path.
world: Mixed codebases are where this lesson pays. A Kotlin domain module holds the model and the bus, and older Java services (a reconciliation job, the support tool, a Temporal worker written with the Java SDK) consume it. Give them Events and the Class<E> overloads, and the Java code reads like any Java library. In Quarkus, a Java CDI bean calling a Kotlin object needs @JvmStatic or it writes INSTANCE everywhere. Run one Java test in the Kotlin module's build, as the lab does, so a Kotlin-side change that breaks Java callers fails on the Kotlin team's own CI instead of in a service owned by another team.
mistake: The common mistake is building the Java door by loosening the model. Someone adds @JvmName("capturedFromJava") to a function that takes PaymentId and Money, or swaps the model's value classes for raw String and Long "so Java can use it". The first lets Java pass a raw long that no init block ever checks: a negative capture gets through. The second brings back the swapped-argument bug for the Kotlin callers too. People do it because it's the quickest way to make javac stop complaining. The fix is a facade that takes plain values and builds the value classes, so every check still runs, and leaves the model alone.

compare.title: The same wiring from Kotlin and from Java

java.title: LedgerWiring.java
java.html: EventBus bus = new EventBus(List.of(new DropDuplicates())); // @JvmOverloads Timings timings = new Timings(); Handler<PaymentEvent> audit = e -> auditLog.add(Events.paymentId(e)); Subscription handle = Events.subscriptions(bus, timings, b -> { // a Consumer: no Unit.INSTANCE b.on(PaymentEvent.class, audit); b.on(PaymentCaptured.class, Handlers.timed(c -> ledger.credit(Events.paymentId(c), Events.amountMinor(c)), "ledger", timings)); b.on(PaymentRefunded.class, Handlers.timed(r -> ledger.debit(Events.paymentId(r), Events.amountMinor(r)), "ledger", timings)); }); bus.publish(Events.captured("pay_7781", 1_999)); // validated by the value classes handle.close(); // close() throws nothing

kotlin.title: LedgerWiring.kt
kotlin.html: val bus = EventBus(listOf(DropDuplicates())) val timings = Timings() val audit = Handler<PaymentEvent> { auditLog += it.paymentId.value } val handle = bus.subscriptions(timings) { on(PaymentEvent::class, audit) timed("ledger") { on<PaymentCaptured> { ledger.credit(it.paymentId, it.amount) } on<PaymentRefunded> { ledger.debit(it.paymentId, it.amount) } } } bus.publish(PaymentCaptured(PaymentId("pay_7781"), Money(1_999))) handle.close()

compare.note: Both wire the same three subscriptions on the same bus, and both get one handle back. The Kotlin version reads the domain types directly (it.paymentId, it.amount), uses on<E> with a reified type and a timed group whose handlers can't reach the outer builder by accident. The Java version passes Class tokens, gets plain String and long through the Events facade, and times handlers one by one with Handlers.timed, because a Kotlin receiver lambda would cost it a return Unit.INSTANCE. What doesn't differ is the safety: the same init blocks validate events built from Java, Handler<? super E> lets the Java audit handler fit any subscription, and javac can switch exhaustively over the Kotlin sealed model.

worked.title: Add subscribeOnce, with its Kotlin sugar and its Java door

steps.say: A welcome email must go out for a merchant's first capture only. Start with the core, in Kotlin, taking a KClass. The handle closes itself, and compareAndSet makes sure only one of eight publishing threads runs the handler, the balking idea from Concurrency patterns that tie it all together. One race needs care: an event can arrive before handle.set has run, so the code closes again after setting it.
steps.code: fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribeOnce(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription { val fired = AtomicBoolean() val handle = AtomicReference<Subscription>() handle.set(subscribe(type) { event -> if (fired.compareAndSet(false, true)) { // 1. only the first event wins try { handler.handle(event) } // 2. do the work finally { handle.get()?.close() } // 3. stop further deliveries } }) if (fired.get()) handle.get().close() // an event won before the handle was set return handle.get() }

alt.html: // What Java sees for the core: a KClass parameter it can only reach the long way round. bus.subscribeOnce(JvmClassMappingKt.getKotlinClass(PaymentCaptured.class), c -> sendWelcome(c));

steps.say: Add the Kotlin sugar: a one-line reified wrapper. No noinline or crossinline: its parameter is a Handler, not a function type, so there is nothing to inline.
steps.code: inline fun <reified E : PaymentEvent> subscribeOnce(handler: Handler<E>): Subscription = subscribeOnce(E::class, handler) bus.subscribeOnce<PaymentCaptured> { sendWelcome(it) }

alt.html: // Java can't see the reified wrapper: javac reports "no suitable method found for subscribeOnce" bus.subscribeOnce(c -> sendWelcome(c));

steps.say: Add the Java door: a Class<E> overload that converts and delegates. Because Handler is declared in, Java sees Handler<? super E>, so a general handler fits too.
steps.code: fun <E : PaymentEvent> subscribeOnce(type: Class<E>, handler: Handler<E>): Subscription = subscribeOnce(type.kotlin, handler)

alt.html: bus.subscribeOnce(PaymentCaptured.class, c -> sendWelcome(Events.paymentId(c)));

steps.say: Last, pin it from both sides. A Kotlin test publishes the same capture from eight threads and checks one email. A Java test makes the Java call above, so a Kotlin-side change that breaks Java callers fails in this module's build.
steps.code: val sent = AtomicInteger() bus.subscribeOnce<PaymentCaptured> { sent.incrementAndGet() } collide(8) { bus.publish(capture) } assertThat(sent.get()).isEqualTo(1)

alt.html: AtomicInteger sent = new AtomicInteger(); bus.subscribeOnce(PaymentCaptured.class, c -> sent.incrementAndGet()); bus.publish(Events.captured("pay_7781", 1_999)); bus.publish(Events.captured("pay_7781", 1_999)); assertThat(sent.get()).isEqualTo(1);

lab.title: Put a DSL and a Java door on the bus
steps: The package starts with lesson 2's solution, already given its Java-facing annotations: @JvmOverloads on the bus constructor, @JvmField on ErrorHandler.PRINT and Ticker.SYSTEM, @file:JvmName("Handlers") on Timing.kt. drill.title: The DSL skeleton and the Java door from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. From memory, write the Kotlin entry function subscriptions, the builder's on(type, handler), commit() and the reified on<E> (with the right modifier). Then, below it, write the Java call that wires one refund handler through Events.subscriptions, and name the annotation or overload behind each part of that Java line.

answer.html: @DslMarker @Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS) annotation class EventsDsl @EventsDsl class SubscriptionsBuilder private constructor(private val bus: EventBus) { private val pending = mutableListOf<Pending<*>>() fun <E : PaymentEvent> on(type: KClass<E>, handler: Handler<E>) { pending += Pending(type, handler) } fun <E : PaymentEvent> on(type: Class<E>, handler: Handler<E>) = on(type.kotlin, handler) inline fun <reified E : PaymentEvent> on(crossinline handler: (E) -> Unit) = on(E::class, Handler { handler(it) }) private fun commit(): Subscription { val handles = pending.map { it.subscribeTo(bus) } return Subscription { handles.asReversed().forEach(Subscription::close) } } private class Pending<E : PaymentEvent>(val type: KClass<E>, val handler: Handler<E>) { fun subscribeTo(bus: EventBus) = bus.subscribe(type, handler) } companion object { fun build(bus: EventBus, block: SubscriptionsBuilder.() -> Unit) = SubscriptionsBuilder(bus).apply(block).commit() } } fun EventBus.subscriptions(block: SubscriptionsBuilder.() -> Unit): Subscription = SubscriptionsBuilder.build(this, block)

alt.html: Subscription handle = Events.subscriptions(bus, b -> // @JvmStatic + a Consumer parameter b.on(PaymentRefunded.class, // the Class<E> overload r -> refunds.add(Events.amountMinor(r)))); // the facade over Money; Handler<? super E> handle.close(); // Subscription.close() throws nothing

recap: A subscription DSL collects what the block declares and subscribes it all at the end: a block that throws subscribes nothing, and one handle closes everything, in reverse order.
on<E> is inline and reified. Its lambda is called from inside a Handler object, so it must be crossinline. A check in on catches subscriptions made from inside a handler, which @DslMarker can't see.
@DslMarker on the builder classes makes only the nearest builder implicit, so timed inside timed stops compiling instead of creating a sibling group.

Java can't call reified functions and stumbles over KClass, defaults, objects, companions and value classes. Add Class<E> overloads, @JvmOverloads, @JvmStatic, @JvmField, @file:JvmName and a facade that builds the value classes, so every check still runs.
Java gets some things for free from earlier choices: Handler<? super E> from in, exhaustive switch over the Kotlin sealed model, and fun interface callbacks that take plain lambdas.
In a design review, a choice an earlier mechanism forces is easy to defend. Write down the judgment calls, and the condition that would make you undo each one.

explain.prompt: A sceptical reviewer says: "This is a lot of type machinery for an event bus. Why not a Map<String, MutableList<(Any) -> Unit>> and a JSON string per event?" Defend your design: name the bugs each choice prevents, and the one or two choices you'd undo.
explain.answer: With strings and Any, every handler parses and casts for itself: a capture with amount "12.50" throws inside the ledger after audit logged it, a typo in an event name never matches, and a new event type is ignored everywhere without a word. The sealed model and the edge parser stop all three: bad input is rejected once, and a when without else breaks the build where a new type needs handling. Value classes make a swapped id and amount a compile error. The bus walks supertypes, so one audit handler sees every event, and Handler<in E> lets that handler fit any subscription from Kotlin and from Java. Isolation, handles and a copy-on-write list keep one bad or self-removing handler from hurting the rest. The DSL commits a block all at once, and @DslMarker keeps nested blocks from reaching the wrong builder. For Java, the overloads and the facade make it read like a Java library without skipping a check. What I'd undo: euro-only Money, as soon as a second currency appears, and the unbounded DropDuplicates, which should become a bounded window or a unique key in the handler's store. And anything that must survive a crash goes to an outbox, not this bus.

deeper.html:
A production version of this library would add, roughly in this order:

  • Asynchronous lanes. An executor per handler group, with one single-threaded lane per payment id so events for one payment keep their order, and a bounded queue in front of each lane. That's also where backpressure lives: when a lane is full, the publisher waits or the event goes to a retry topic.
  • Real metrics and tracing. Replace Timings with Micrometer timers named after the subscription, and carry the trace context from the Kafka record through publish into each handler, so a slow handler shows up in the trace of the request that caused it.
  • Durability. Events that must survive a crash or reach other services go through a transactional outbox to Kafka, as Observer and Command described. The in-process bus stays for decoupling modules inside one service.
  • Dead letters for the edge. Parsed.Rejected goes to a dead-letter topic with the reason, a counter, and a replay tool for after the fix.
  • Versioned events. Stable type names with @SerialName if you serialize with kotlinx.serialization, and parser branches that map old names to new types.
  • A checked public API. on<E> and subscribe<E> are public inline functions, so their bodies are compiled into every caller, and the @JvmOverloads overloads are part of the Java ABI. A binary-compatibility check in the build catches a change that would break callers compiled against the previous version.
  • @JvmExposeBoxed once it is stable, if it also covers interface members. Until then, the Events facade is the Java door.

One thing it should not add is reflection-driven registration with annotations, Guava style (@Subscribe on methods, found by scanning). Guava's own Javadoc lists the costs: subscribers are hard to find from the publisher, and reflection breaks under code shrinkers. Explicit on<E> calls keep every subscription visible in the code that owns it.
